input.question: If one company buys out another company for a monetary fee, wouldn’t the money go back to the parent company, therefore the parent company essentially gained capital for free since they own the other company? How does that work?
input.ground_truth: No, because when the company is bought it is bought from its owners. You know, the shareholders? They get the money from the buyout. The only way it would stay with the company is if the company owned itself which is silly.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: If one company buys out another company for a monetary fee, wouldn’t the money go back to the parent company, therefore the parent company essentially gained capital for free since they own the other company? How does that work?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine you have a lemonade stand (that’s your first company), and your big brother has a toy store (that’s the parent company).

Now, your big brother really likes your lemonade stand, so he decides to buy it from you. He gives you some money for it. That money goes into your piggy bank.

But here’s the thing: your big brother already owns the toy store, and now he also owns your lemonade stand. So now, he has two businesses, and he used some of his own money (from his piggy bank) to buy the lemonade stand.

It doesn’t mean he got money for free. He gave up some of his own money to buy the lemonade stand. Now, he hopes that the lemonade stand will make even more money, so that the money he spent will grow bigger over time. But he didn’t get money for free—he paid for it.

So, when a big company buys a smaller company, they use their own money to pay for it. They hope the smaller company will help them make even more money in the future. They don’t get money for free—they spend it!
